raw_json.title: Agent auto-persists referenceable/feature-specific knowledge into always-loaded global memory, inflating per-turn context cost
raw_json.body:
- Copilot Chat Extension Version: 0.x (current, June 2026)
- VS Code Version: 1.127.x
- OS Version: Windows 11
- Feature: agent mode — memory tool (auto-write behavior)
- Selected model: Claude (Opus/Sonnet class)
- Logs: see measured evidence below

### Shared context (this issue has a sibling: #323167)
Both this issue and #323167 stem from the memory feature operating silently/automatically. The auto-write behavior described here continually grows /memories/ files, and the corruption bug in #323167 then multiplies that content — so the two compound each other (silent context bloat + data corruption).

### Core defect
In agent mode the model auto-persists **feature-specific and already-referenceable knowledge** into **always-loaded global memory** (`/memories/`). The first ~200 lines of user/global memory are injected into context on **every turn, in every workspace**, indefinitely. This is the wrong storage tier for this kind of content, for three reasons:

1. **Duplication of referenceable knowledge.** Feature details that already live in retrievable `docs/` files (or repo memory) get copied into always-loaded memory. The same information that a one-time on-demand `read_file` could supply *only when relevant* is instead injected into context on every turn forever. Same data, loaded continuously instead of on access — negative value.

2. **No relevance scoping.** Global memory loads in every workspace regardless of topic. A partner servicing N customers ends up loading, in customer X's sessions, customer Y's feature notes. Even within a single app, knowledge for feature A is loaded while working on unrelated feature B.

3. **Unbounded time cost.** A feature you don't touch for 3–4 years is still loaded on every turn in the interim, with zero corresponding use, and nothing ages it out.

### The principle being violated
Always-loaded persistent memory should hold only **small, cross-cutting, non-referenceable** facts (durable preferences, hard-won gotchas). Anything that is **(a) already retrievable from a doc, or (b) feature/workspace-specific** should NOT be auto-written to global memory — it should stay in `docs/` (or at most repo-scoped, on-demand memory) and be pulled only when relevant. The current `<memoryInstructions>` ("record what you learned") pushes the agent to do the opposite.

### Reproduced cross-workspace leak (captured this session)
I have a multi-root setup with separate workspaces. One workspace contains **only** a Business Central (AL) app and has **no knowledge of, and no files from, a separate React Native mobile app**. From that BC-only workspace I asked the agent — explicitly forbidding it from searching or reading any files — what it knew about the mobile app's PO-extraction work.

It answered with mobile/Python-pipeline feature specifics (`operating_pressure_psi` as a per-`part_item` schema field, the Phase A/B/C structure, a "mobile applier" that reads `shipping_resolved.agent_code/service_code` and falls back to `carrierHint`/`serviceLevelHint` on `csr_confirm`) and **explicitly attributed all of it to an auto-loaded global memory note**, `PO-Extract-Phase2-Handoff.md`. Verbatim from its reply:

> "Where the knowledge came from: Entirely from my persistent user-memory file … specifically the auto-loaded note `PO-Extraction-Phase2-Handoff.md` (under user memory). Nothing here came from reading the workspace, `app/docs/`, or any `.ts`/`.tsx` file in this session."

Notably it also correctly declined to fabricate the parts the note didn't contain — so the attribution is credible, not a hallucination. This is a concrete demonstration that feature-specific notes from one workspace are loaded into an unrelated workspace's context, with zero relevance to the task at hand.

### Measured evidence (real machine, single user)
- User/global memory: 26,438 bytes ≈ 6,610 tokens, auto-loaded every turn, every workspace
- Much of it is feature-specific content that already exists in this repo's `docs/` (e.g. PO-extraction internals) — i.e. duplicated, not unique
- All memory across all workspaces: 24 files, 156,069 bytes ≈ 39,017 tokens
- Example of mis-tiered content: workspace-specific feature notes (`phys-inv-*`, `PO-Extract-*`) auto-written to globally-loaded memory rather than left in retrievable docs

### Cost / impact (corrected — important)
The primary cost on a **GitHub Copilot subscription is NOT direct dollars.** Copilot meters by **premium request, not tokens** — one prompt in agent mode = one premium request × the model's multiplier, with tool calls and autonomous steps excluded, and overage billed per request ($0.04/request). Token volume inside a request does not change the billed amount. So on Copilot the real cost of this bloat is:

- **Context-window dilution and answer-quality degradation** — every turn spends a fixed slice of the window on irrelevant, often duplicated, cross-workspace notes.
- **Compounding with #323167** — corrupted/duplicated memory enlarges that always-loaded slice further.

The dollar cost only materializes under **per-token billing (Anthropic API / BYOK)**. As an order-of-magnitude reference there: ~6,610 tokens × ~420 sessions/month ≈ ~2.8M input tokens/month; at an Opus-class list rate of roughly $15 / 1M input tokens that is on the order of ~$40/month — but this does NOT apply to a standard Copilot subscription, where the same usage is $0 at the margin.

2. **Relevance-scope what is loaded** — don't inject every workspace's notes into every other workspace's context.
3. **Age out / cap** stale entries, and surface the memory store's size and context footprint in the UI.
4. Allow `copilot-instructions.md` / project config to suppress or constrain memory writes (ref #308669).
5. (Secondary) make global memory writes opt-in or per-write confirmable.

### Steps to reproduce
1. Use agent mode normally over several sessions with the memory tool available, in a multi-root / multi-workspace setup.
2. Observe that feature-specific notes — content that already exists in retrievable `docs/` — are auto-written to `/memories/` without an explicit request to "save this."
3. From an unrelated workspace, ask the agent (forbidding file reads) about a feature that only exists in another workspace; it will recite it from auto-loaded global memory and attribute it to that note.

- #308669 — `<memoryInstructions>` cannot be overridden by copilot-instructions.md

I also found another issue like when I opened VS Code without connecting to Internet and then later on connected to Internet and try to Prompt and start conversation with other Provider the connection and generation isn't happening with that provider rather it is using copilot models and generating the output. Both these Issues found in different times and testing multiple times, not once. title: Warn when NaN is passed as an aria-* attribute value
content:
## Summary

aria-* attributes currently bypass the NaN check in `ReactDOMUnknownPropertyHook` because they return early (line 97-99 of that file) before the check is reached. When a `NaN` number flows through, the DOM stringifies it to the literal string `"NaN"`, which is invalid for **every** ARIA attribute type and silently breaks accessibility.

This is a common pitfall when a computed numeric value is derived from user data or state that can be undefined/null:

```jsx
// e.g. items.findIndex(...) returns -1 → some derived math → NaN
<div aria-valuenow={computedValue} />  // renders aria-valuenow="NaN" — silent bug
```

**Changes:**

- `ReactDOMInvalidARIAHook.js` — extend `validateProperty` to accept the prop `value` and add a `NaN` check for valid, correctly-cased aria-* attributes. Mirrors the warning message already used by `ReactDOMUnknownPropertyHook` for non-aria attributes.
- `ReactDOMInvalidARIAHook-test.js` — three new test cases: NaN on a numeric aria attribute (`aria-valuenow`), NaN on a string-type aria attribute (`aria-label`), and no false-positive for valid integers.

## Test plan

- [x] `yarn test ReactDOMInvalidARIAHook` — all tests pass (new + existing)
- [x] Existing tests unaffected — only the `validateProperty` signature changes (internal)

When a `NaN` number flows through, the DOM stringifies it to the literal string `"NaN"`, which is invalid for **every** ARIA attribute type and silently breaks accessibility.

This is a common pitfall when a computed numeric value is derived from user data or state that can be undefined/null:

```jsx
// e.g. items.findIndex(...) returns -1 → some derived math → NaN
<div aria-valuenow={computedValue} />  // renders aria-valuenow="NaN" — silent bug
```

**Changes:**

- `ReactDOMInvalidARIAHook.js` — extend `validateProperty` to accept the prop `value` and add a `NaN` check for valid, correctly-cased aria-* attributes. Mirrors the warning message already used by `ReactDOMUnknownPropertyHook` for non-aria attributes.
- `ReactDOMInvalidARIAHook-test.js` — three new test cases: NaN on a numeric aria attribute (`aria-valuenow`), NaN on a string-type aria attribute (`aria-label`), and no false-positive for valid integers.

## Test plan

- [x] `yarn test ReactDOMInvalidARIAHook` — all tests pass (new + existing)
- [x] Existing tests unaffected — only the `validateProperty` signature changes (internal)

title: Fix false hydration mismatch when client renders portal that returned null on server
content:
## Summary

Fixes #12615

When a component returns `null` on the server but renders a `ReactDOM.createPortal()` on the client, React was incorrectly emitting a hydration mismatch error:

```
Hydration failed because the server rendered HTML didn't match the client.
  <span>
    <HoverMenu>
+     <div>   ← false positive: this is portal content, not a span child
```

This is a false positive — the portal's `<div>` renders into a **separate container**, not into the parent `<span>`. It should not be compared against the parent's server HTML.

## Root Cause

When `updatePortalComponent` calls `pushHostContainer` to switch to the portal's container, the hydration state variables (`isHydrating`, `nextHydratableInstance`, `hydrationParentFiber`) were not reset. The portal's children then tried to claim hydration instances from the **parent container's** server nodes, which failed and triggered a mismatch error.

## Fix

Added two functions to `ReactFiberHydrationContext`:

- **`prepareToHydrateHostPortal`** — called in `updatePortalComponent` (begin work). Saves the current hydration state onto a stack and resets it, so portal children are inserted fresh rather than matched against server HTML.
- **`popHydrationStateAfterPortal`** — called in the `HostPortal` case of complete work. Restores the saved hydration state so the parent resumes hydrating correctly after the portal.

This correctly handles nested portals (via the stack) and cleans up on `resetHydrationState` (work loop interruption).

## Test Plan

- Added two new tests in `ReactDOMHydrationDiff-test.js`:
  - Portal renders to a separate container → no mismatch warning
  - Portal renders to the hydration root container → no mismatch warning
- All 39 hydration diff tests pass
- All 183 tests across `ReactServerRenderingHydration`, `ReactDOMServerPartialHydration`, and `ReactDOMFiber` suites pass

title: [compiler] Fix refs validation for forwarded ref props
content:
Fixes #35997

## Summary

This fixes a false positive in `react-hooks/refs` when forwarding a `ref` prop directly to JSX.

Previously, code like:

```tsx
function TextArea(props) {
  return <TextInput ref={props.ref} type="body" />;
}
```

was reported as:

`Cannot access refs during render`

even though the component was only forwarding the ref object to JSX and not reading `ref.current`.

The root cause was that `ValidateNoRefAccessInRender` validated all JSX attribute operands uniformly. That was too strict for the special `ref` prop, where passing a ref object through to JSX should be allowed.

This change teaches the validator to treat JSX `ref` attributes specially:

- still validate the JSX tag
- still validate non-`ref` JSX attributes
- still validate spread attributes and children
- skip direct-ref-value validation for the `ref` attribute itself

This preserves the existing error for actual render-time ref reads like `props.ref.current`, while allowing valid ref forwarding patterns.

## How did you test this change?

Reproduced the issue with a focused compiler fixture:

1. Add a fixture containing:

```js
// @validateRefAccessDuringRender @compilationMode:"infer"
function TextArea(props) {
  return <TextInput ref={props.ref} type="body" />;
}
```

2. Run:

```bash
corepack yarn workspace babel-plugin-react-compiler snap --pattern allow-forwarding-ref-prop-to-jsx --sync
```

Before the fix, this failed with:

```text
Error: Cannot access refs during render
...
return <TextInput ref={props.ref} type="body" />;
                         ^^^^^^^^^ Cannot access ref value during render
```

After the fix, the same targeted fixture passes:

```bash
corepack yarn workspace babel-plugin-react-compiler snap --pattern allow-forwarding-ref-prop-to-jsx --sync
```

I also checked the existing invalid fixture for reading `props.ref.current` to confirm the validator still rejects direct ref-value access during render.

title: [Flight] Performance track debug info is not recovered for plain object roots
content:
## Summary

`flushComponentPerformance` reads `root._debugInfo` from the chunk. When
that array is empty and the chunk is fulfilled, it recovers the debug info
from the resolved value, but only when the value is an array, an async
iterable, a React element, or a lazy:

```js
if (debugInfo.length === 0 && root.status === 'fulfilled') {
  const resolvedValue = resolveLazy(root.value);
  if (
    typeof resolvedValue === 'object' && resolvedValue !== null &&
    (isArray(resolvedValue) ||
      typeof resolvedValue[ASYNC_ITERATOR] === 'function' ||
      resolvedValue.$$typeof === REACT_ELEMENT_TYPE ||
      resolvedValue.$$typeof === REACT_LAZY_TYPE) &&
    isArray(resolvedValue._debugInfo)
  ) {
    debugInfo = resolvedValue._debugInfo;
  }
}
```

A plain object root is excluded, so the Server Components track in the
Performance panel does not work for payloads whose root is a plain object,
even when the resolved value carries a `_debugInfo` array. Verified in
`react-server-dom-webpack@19.3.0-canary-28cd4bb0-20260723`.

## Context

Waku's RSC payload root is a plain object mapping slot ids to elements
(`Record<string, unknown>`), which lets one payload carry several named
elements. This shape is deliberate and we would like to keep it. Today we
patch the read site with a build transform that drops the type restriction,
which works but is coupled to the compiled output:

https://github.com/wakujs/waku/blob/main/packages/waku/src/lib/vite-plugins/patch-rsdw.ts

@vitejs/plugin-rsc documents the same shape constraint for its performance
track example (vitejs/vite-plugin-react#1152, vitejs/vite-plugin-react#1304).

## Request

Relax the recovery to accept any object value that carries an own
`_debugInfo` array. The type restriction seems to mirror
`moveDebugInfoFromChunkToInnerValue`, where it guards attaching
`_debugInfo` to the value. The read site only reads the property, so the
restriction does not appear to protect anything there, and the relaxation
is additive: values without `_debugInfo` behave as before.

If there is a supported way to get the performance track with a plain
object root without reshaping the payload, that guidance would also
resolve this for us.

Release notes

Sourced from axios's releases.

v1.18.1 — June 21, 2026

This release focuses on Node HTTP adapter fixes, safer AxiosError serialisation, runtime/type correctness fixes, documentation updates, and dependency maintenance.

🐛 Bug Fixes

  • AxiosError Serialisation: Made AxiosError#cause non-enumerable to prevent circular JSON serialisation failures when errors include nested causes. (#10913)
  • Node HTTP Adapter: Guarded socket.setKeepAlive for proxy agent streams, accepted path-only URLs when socketPath is configured, deferred environment proxy handling to Node, and explicitly passed maxBodyLength through to follow-redirects. (#10917, #10930, #10942, #10993)
  • Runtime and Type Correctness: Fixed several runtime crashes, type definition mismatches, and incorrect error handling paths. (#10959, #11021)
  • AxiosURLSearchParams: Switched the encoder callback to an arrow function so encoder.call(this) receives the AxiosURLSearchParams instance correctly. (#11019)

🔧 Maintenance & Chores

  • Documentation: Documented sensitive headers and status transition behaviour, prepared cleaned-up docs, added Deno install instructions, and clarified that request data is request-specific (#11007, #11010, #11023, #11025)

  • Dependencies: Bumped vite, rollup, form-data, js-yaml, and multer across the root project, docs, smoke tests, and module test workspaces. (#11011, #11012, #11013, #11014, #11015, #11016, #11017, #11026)

🌟 New Contributors

We are thrilled to welcome our new contributors. Thank you for helping improve axios:

  • @​webdevelopersrinu (#10913)

Full Changelog

v1.18.0 — June 13, 2026

This release hardens redirect and URL handling, improves the validateStatus configuration semantics, and includes updates to documentation, dependencies, and release metadata.

🔒 Security Fixes

  • Redirect Header Safety: Added Node HTTP adapter support for stripping caller-specified sensitive headers on cross-origin redirects, helping prevent custom auth headers such as API keys from leaking to another origin. (#10892)

  • URL And Request Hardening: Rejects malformed http: and https: URLs that omit // with ERR_INVALID_URL, while tightening prototype-pollution-safe config reads, stream size limits, FormData depth handling, data URL sizing, and local NO_PROXY matching. (#11000)

🐛 Bug Fixes

  • Status Validation: Added transitional.validateStatusUndefinedResolves so applications can opt in to treating validateStatus: undefined like the option was omitted, while validateStatus: null remains the explicit way to accept every status. (#10899)

title: [verified] fix(reconciler): recheck store snapshot after subscribe
content:
## Summary
- Problem: `useSyncExternalStore` can miss a post-subscribe snapshot repair when `Suspense` + `StrictMode` remounts a store consumer and the store mutates during `subscribe()` without notifying listeners.
- Why it matters: the hook contract expects a snapshot re-check after subscribing, but this remount path skipped that repair step.
- What changed: `subscribeToStore(...)` now re-checks the snapshot immediately after `subscribe(handleStoreChange)` returns and forces a rerender if the store changed during subscribe.
- What did NOT change (scope boundary): this does not change broader Suspense replay semantics or attempt to guarantee that no stale intermediate render is ever observed before the repair rerender.

## How did you test this change?
- `CI=1 npx -y yarn test useSyncExternalStore-test --runInBand`
- `CI=1 npx -y yarn test useSyncExternalStore --runInBand`

Related to: https://github.com/facebook/react/issues/35550

- What changed: `subscribeToStore(...)` now re-checks the snapshot immediately after `subscribe(handleStoreChange)` returns and forces a rerender if the store changed during subscribe.
- What did NOT change (scope boundary): this does not change broader Suspense replay semantics or attempt to guarantee that no stale intermediate render is ever observed before the repair rerender.

## How did you test this change?
- `CI=1 npx -y yarn test useSyncExternalStore-test --runInBand`
- `CI=1 npx -y yarn test useSyncExternalStore --runInBand`

title: [DOM] Guard window.event reads in scheduler event tracking
content:
## Summary

Fixes #37100.

The DEV-only Performance Tracks instrumentation added in 19.2.0 reads `window.event` unconditionally in `trackSchedulerEvent()`, `resolveEventType()`, and `resolveEventTimeStamp()`. `trackSchedulerEvent()` runs at the entry of Scheduler-driven tasks (`performWorkOnRootViaSchedulerTask`, `processRootScheduleInImmediateTask`, and the passive-effects flush scheduled by `commitRoot`). These tasks live on deferred `setImmediate` ticks and can legitimately fire after a per-test-file DOM environment (jsdom / happy-dom under vitest or jest) has been torn down. When that happens the task throws `ReferenceError: window is not defined` before doing any work, which fails entire CI suites with an unhandled error attributed to the next, innocent test file.

This guards the three reads with `typeof window !== 'undefined'`, matching the bundle's existing convention for `window` accesses that may run outside a browser DOM (e.g. `canUseDOM`, the `window.ErrorEvent` detection in the error-reporting path). When `window` is gone the attribution resolves to `undefined`, i.e. "no event", which is accurate. `shouldAttemptEagerTransition()` and `resolveUpdatePriority()` are left untouched: they only run while an update is being dispatched, so `window` is alive by construction there.

## How did you test this change?

- Added a regression test (`ReactDOMWindowTeardown-test.js`, node environment + manually constructed JSDOM mirroring the issue's repro). It fails on `main` with `ReferenceError: window is not defined` from `performWorkOnRootViaSchedulerTask` and passes with this change.
- `yarn test ReactPerformanceTrack ReactDOMFiberAsync ReactDOMNativeEventHeuristic` — all pass.
- `yarn linc`, `yarn flow dom-node`, `yarn prettier` — clean.
- Ran the repro script from #37100 verbatim: against published `react-dom@19.2.8` it crashes as reported; against a locally built `NODE_DEV` bundle with this change it prints `done, no crash` and exits 0.

title: [Fiber] Don't reaquire HostSingletons during dev effect validation
content:
Stacked on #37112

In dev effects are validated using a double-invoke technique. To do this the effects are destroyed and recreated during a validation traversal. However this same disappear and reappear path is used when Offscreen Fibers go hidden and HostSingletons have unique behavior when going hidden. So now that the double invoke effects process happens during hydration it is more common to have your Singletons be released and acquired during this validation phase which is observable most notably by having extra attributes removed from them. The prior commits in this stack deal with preserving non-react owned attributes on release however it is semantically incorrect to release and acquire the singleton during this validation because it isn't really an effect, it simply lives in this traversal to avoid having to do another traversal during the commit.

This change adds a bit of info to the release and acquire path to only conditionally perform the necessary reacquire flow if we are not in the validation phase.

title: [Fiber] only remove properties from singletons on release
content:
Removing attributes does not actually reset all property state on the singleton instance. It also has the side effect of wiping any 3rd party set attributes and properties that 3rd party scripts and extensions.

Reimplements the singleton release to clear properties on the instance based on the last committed props for the singleton fiber.

Notably there is an unfixed path with preamble contribution markers that still just clears based on attributes which covers SSR'd attributes that need to be wiped before client recovery on hydration can continue. There are gated failing tests for this as a TODO.

go version go1.26.5 linux/amd64

### Output of `go env` in your module/workspace:

```shell
GOPROXY='https://proxy.golang.org,direct'
GOROOT='/opt/hostedtoolcache/go-6d471830/1.26.5/x64'
GOSUMDB='sum.golang.org'
GOTELEMETRY='local'
GOTELEMETRYDIR='/home/runner/.config/go/telemetry'
GOTMPDIR=''
GOTOOLCHAIN='local'
GOTOOLDIR='/opt/hostedtoolcache/go-6d471830/1.26.5/x64/pkg/tool/linux_amd64'
GOVCS=''
GOVERSION='go1.26.5'
GOWORK=''
PKG_CONFIG='pkg-config'
```

### What did you do?

An HTTP/2 `StreamError` can escape from one `net/http` transport through `Response.Body.Read`. If that body is used as the backing connection for another HTTP/2 transport, the outer transport mistakes the underlying error for a stream error parsed on the outer connection.

The following program uses only the standard library. It obtains a real net/http.http2StreamError from an inner HTTP/2 request, then returns it as a sticky read error from the connection backing an outer HTTP/2 request.

https://go.dev/play/p/IMjFU6ArpRU

(Should run this locally; running it on the playground will result in a deadlock error.)

Output:

```
inner error: http.http2StreamError: stream error: stream ID 1; INTERNAL_ERROR; received from peer
underlying Read calls in 100ms: 2253786
```

The process consumes approximately one CPU core until the connection is explicitly closed.

A real-world example is an in-process HTTP client running HTTP/2 over a `net.Conn` implemented using another HTTP/2 response body. No custom construction of the private error type is required.

### What did you see happen?

The outer HTTP/2 read loop continues reading after the underlying connection returns `http2StreamError`.

`Framer.ReadFrameHeader` and `ReadFrameForHeader` return errors from the underlying reader unchanged. The client read loop then performs a direct type assertion:
```golang
if se, ok := err.(http2StreamError); ok {
	if cs := rl.streamByID(se.StreamID, http2notHeaderOrDataFrame); cs != nil {
		rl.endStreamError(cs, se)
	}
	continue
}
```

This assumes every `http2StreamError` was produced while parsing the current connection. An error originating from a lower HTTP/2 transport has the same concrete type, so it is treated as recoverable.

If the lower reader retains the error, as HTTP/2 response bodies and TLS connections may do, every subsequent read returns the same error and the loop spins indefinitely.

The server-side `terminalReadFrameError` check appears to have the same provenance issue.

### What did you expect to see?

A `StreamError` generated by the current Framer should remain recoverable and affect only its stream.

A `StreamError` returned by the `Framer`'s underlying `io.Reader` should be treated as a terminal connection read error. The read loop should exit and close the connection rather than reading again.

### Suggested fix

Distinguish errors originating from the underlying reader at the Framer I/O boundary. One minimal approach is to wrap only reader-provided `StreamError` values:

```golang
type frameReadError struct {
	err error
}

func (e frameReadError) Error() string { return e.err.Error() }
func (e frameReadError) Unwrap() error { return e.err }

type framerReader struct {
	io.Reader
}

func (r framerReader) Read(p []byte) (n int, err error) {
	n, err = r.Reader.Read(p)
	if _, ok := err.(StreamError); ok {
		err = frameReadError{err: err}
	}
	return n, err
}
```

The `Framer` constructor can wrap its reader once:
```golang
if r != nil {
	r = framerReader{Reader: r}
}
```

This covers frame headers, payloads, and recursive CONTINUATION reads. Locally parsed `StreamError` values remain direct values, while reader-originated errors become terminal to the existing direct type checks.

The wrapper preserves the error text and supports `errors.As` through `Unwrap`.

Regression tests should cover both cases:

The underlying reader returns `StreamError` while reading a frame header.
A valid frame header is read, then the underlying reader returns `StreamError` while reading the payload.
In both cases, the error should unwrap to `StreamError` but must be considered terminal by the HTTP/2 read loop.


### What did you do?

I built the following reproducer program for mips64le, and ran it in qemu, it produced a crash with a trace identical to 
https://github.com/golang/go/issues/80557 and https://github.com/golang/go/issues/80560

```go
package main

import "fmt"

type params struct{ k, l int }

var sink byte
var arr [56]uint32

//go:noinline
func fill(b []byte) {
	for i := range b {
		b[i] = byte(i)
	}
}

//go:noinline
func newThing(p params) []uint32 {
	// kl is computed in the entry block (kept there because it has uses in
	// two different blocks), lives in LO across the call to fill, and so
	// must be spilled from LO. The spill slot lands beyond the 32KB reach
	// of a MIPS 16-bit signed load/store offset because of scratch.
	kl := p.k * p.l
	var scratch [33000]byte
	if p.k > 0 {
		fill(scratch[:])
		sink = scratch[99]
		return arr[:kl]
	}
	return arr[kl:]
}

func main() {
	s := newThing(params{4, 4})
	fmt.Println("ok:", len(s))
}
```


```
GOROOT=/home/daniel/Code/Go/golang GOOS=linux GOARCH=mips64le /home/daniel/Code/Go/golang/bin/go build -o repro main.go
qemu-mips64el ./repro
```



### What did you see happen?

```
panic: runtime error: slice bounds out of range [:131666012437824] with length 56

goroutine 1 [running]:
main.newThing({0x4, 0x4})
	/tmp/mipsrepro/main.go:28 +0x1bc
main.main()
	/tmp/mipsrepro/main.go:34 +0x44
```

This also reproduces outside of qemu on a `mips64le` gomote.

### What did you expect to see?


I expected to see no index out of bounds runtime error and the output `ok:16`.

Building the same reproduction program for my native arch (x86_64) instead of MIPS & running it produces this result.

I believe (_FWIW, claude assisted here_) that the issue is that regalloc can spill a multiply result from the LO special register. That spill routes through REGTMP (R23) but when the frame exceeds 32KB, the assembler also needs REGTMP to materialize the store offset, clobbering the value with SP+0x10000. That matches up with the bogus index in the panic traces.

I think this manifested in https://github.com/golang/go/issues/80560 and https://github.com/golang/go/issues/80557 because of the very chonky 33kb stack frame for `mldsa.newPrivateKey`:

```
GOROOT=/home/daniel/Code/Go/golang GOOS=linux GOARCH=mips64le /home/daniel/Code/Go/golang/bin/go build -gcflags=-S crypto/internal/fips140/mldsa 2>&1 | sed -n '/TEXT.*newPrivateKey/,/STEXT/p' | grep -E 'TEXT|mldsa.go:186' | head -n1
	0x0000 00000 (/home/daniel/Code/Go/golang/src/crypto/internal/fips140/mldsa/mldsa.go:172)	TEXT	crypto/internal/fips140/mldsa.newPrivateKey(SB), ABIInternal, $31304-80
```

title: os: running SameFile on two character files or pipes will always return true on Windows
content:
### Go version

go version go1.26.4 windows/amd64

### Output of `go env` in your module/workspace:

```shell
set AR=ar
set CC=gcc
set CGO_CFLAGS=-O2 -g
set CGO_CPPFLAGS=
set CGO_CXXFLAGS=-O2 -g
set CGO_ENABLED=0
set CGO_FFLAGS=-O2 -g
set CGO_LDFLAGS=-O2 -g
set CXX=g++
set GCCGO=gccgo
set GO111MODULE=
set GOAMD64=v1
set GOARCH=amd64
set GOAUTH=netrc
set GOBIN=
set GOCACHE=C:\Users\<REDACTED>\AppData\Local\go-build
set GOCACHEPROG=
set GODEBUG=
set GOENV=C:\Users\<REDACTED>\AppData\Roaming\go\env
set GOEXE=.exe
set GOEXPERIMENT=
set GOFIPS140=off
set GOFLAGS=
set GOGCCFLAGS=-m64 -fno-caret-diagnostics -Qunused-arguments -Wl,--no-gc-sections -fmessage-length=0 -ffile-prefix-map=C:\Users\<REDACTED>\AppData\Local\Temp\go-build3940039365=/tmp/go-build -gno-record-gcc-switches
set GOHOSTARCH=amd64
set GOHOSTOS=windows
set GOINSECURE=
set GOMOD=NUL
set GOMODCACHE=C:\Users\<REDACTED>\go\pkg\mod
set GONOPROXY=
set GONOSUMDB=
set GOOS=windows
set GOPATH=C:\Users\<REDACTED>\go
set GOPRIVATE=
set GOPROXY=https://proxy.golang.org,direct
set GOROOT=C:\Users\<REDACTED>\scoop\apps\go\current
set GOSUMDB=sum.golang.org
set GOTELEMETRY=local
set GOTELEMETRYDIR=C:\Users\<REDACTED>\AppData\Roaming\go\telemetry
set GOTMPDIR=
set GOTOOLCHAIN=auto
set GOTOOLDIR=C:\Users\<REDACTED>\scoop\apps\go\current\pkg\tool\windows_amd64
set GOVCS=
set GOVERSION=go1.26.4
set GOWORK=
set PKG_CONFIG=pkg-config
```

### What did you do?

```go
package main

import (
   "os"
   "fmt"
)

func main() {
   con, _ := os.Create("CONOUT$")
   defer con.Close()
   
   fmt.Fprintln(os.Stdout, "This is stdout")
   fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "This is stderr")
   
   infOut, _ := os.Stdout.Stat()
   infErr, _ := os.Stderr.Stat()
   fmt.Fprintf(con, "Stdout and Stderr are same file: %v\n", os.SameFile(infOut, infErr))
}
```
This was put in a go file and built into an executable called `bugTest.exe` on Windows

### What did you see happen?

This what I see when I run these commands in the Windows command prompt
```
-->bugTest
This is stdout
This is stderr
Stdout and Stderr are same file: true

-->bugTest > nul
This is stderr
Stdout and Stderr are same file: true

-->
```

### What did you expect to see?

If the `os.SameFile` function is run on Windows, and both files are either pipes or character files, the function will always return `true`, even when the files/pipes are different. In the output in the command prompt, the first command invocation works as expected, since both stdout and stderr are direccted to the console, they represent the same file/pipe. But when stdout is redirected to `nul`, the SameFile function still reports `true`, even though stdout is redirected, but stderr still points to the console output.

Here we can see when the `Stat` function is called, if the file type is a character type or a pipe, only the `name` and `filetype` fields of the `fileStat` struct are set

https://github.com/golang/go/blob/03845e30f7b73d1703bd8c21017297f6eecb76d6/src/os/stat_windows.go#L108-L116

Then the `sameFile` function calls `loadFileId` on each `fileStat` struct

https://github.com/golang/go/blob/03845e30f7b73d1703bd8c21017297f6eecb76d6/src/os/types_windows.go#L353-L363

`loadFileId` sees that fs.path is an empty string and returns before setting `fs.vol`, `fs.idxhi`, and `fs.idxlo`

https://github.com/golang/go/blob/03845e30f7b73d1703bd8c21017297f6eecb76d6/src/os/types_windows.go#L287-L293

This is explained here

https://github.com/golang/go/blob/03845e30f7b73d1703bd8c21017297f6eecb76d6/src/os/types_windows.go#L75-L77

Now the `vol`, `idxhi`, and `idxlo` fields have never been set, so they will always be 0 for any character file or pipe, so any two character files or pipes will always claim to be the same file.

As far as I know there isn't a way on Windows to determine if two character files or pipes are the same, since [GetFileInformationByHandle](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/fileapi/nf-fileapi-getfileinformationbyhandle) can't be called on these types of files. If someone more familiar with the Windows API than me knows better I'd be gladly corrected. But I definitely don't think returning `true` is the correct thing to do here. It seems that the convention is that when `os.SameFile` returns `true` that is a guarantee that the two files are the same, but when it returns `false` that doesn't guarantee that they are distinct. I think ideally there would be a function that could tell you whether two files were definitely the same, definitely distinct, or whether their distinctness could not be determined, but that's not what we have, unfortunately

As far as I know this bug has existed since https://github.com/golang/go/commit/ebd67ba588eabd5bf968b5bd14dff21a1a1b1be4 in some form, and has just not been noticed.

A way that I think would fix the issue would be to change

https://github.com/golang/go/blob/03845e30f7b73d1703bd8c21017297f6eecb76d6/src/os/stat_windows.go#L115
to 
```go
return &fileStat{name: filepathlite.Base(name), filetype: ft, path: name}, nil
```
but I don't know if that might cause other issues, of if that's the best approach

title: cmd/compile/internal/ssa: elide redundant 32-bit zero extensions on arm64
content:
ZeroUpper32Bits knows about arm64's W-form ALU results, but not about its
zero-extending loads and register moves. The late lower rule
(MOVWUreg x) && ZeroUpper32Bits(x, 3) => x therefore never fires for a
value that came from MOVWUload/MOVHUload/MOVBUload or from a narrower
MOV*Ureg.

With a single use the extension still folds away, via
(MOVWUreg x:(MOVWUload _ _)) => (MOVDreg x) and

title: cmd/go: Regression in Go 1.26 due to new pkg-config flag validation from #77387 banning safe `--define-variable` values
content:
### Go version

go version go1.26.3 linux/amd64

### Output of `go env` in your module/workspace:

```shell
n/a
```

### What did you do?

Upgrade from Go 1.25 to Go 1.26

### What did you see happen?

An existing build started failing with:
```
foobar/core/foobar/protocol/foobar/common: invalid flag in pkg-config: --define-variable=srcdir=/home/tcagent3/opt/teamcity/work/tech-build/foobar/tech/core/foobar/protocol/foobar/common (see https://go.dev/s/invalidflag)
```

Upon investigation, it seems that the fix for #77387 has resulted in banning safe flag values in pkg-config files, namely those that define variables with values containing dash characters, amongst others.

I am guessing that the regex at https://github.com/golang/go/blob/2403e594a5b279bd7b393c32f74528fd4ef29c4a/src/cmd/go/internal/work/security.go#L262 was intended to be something slightly different.

The outcome is that I am no longer able to build this (internal) software without ensuring there is no dash character anywhere in the absolute pathname containing the build environment, though other users may be impacted in other ways depending on the purpose for which they were using variables.

### What did you expect to see?

No regression.

title: Cap socket send length to c_int::MAX on Apple targets
content:
On Apple, `send`/`sendto` reject a length larger than `c_int::MAX` with `EINVAL` instead of doing a short send. The send length was only clamped to `wrlen_t::MAX` (a no-op on 64-bit unix), so writing more than `c_int::MAX` bytes to a socket failed on macOS.

Add a `MAX_SEND_LEN` cap (`c_int::MAX` on Apple, `wrlen_t::MAX` elsewhere), used in `write`, `send`, `send_to`, and `send_with_flags`.

Fixes rust-lang/rust#115325

title: Add -Zmips-nan2008 to enable IEEE 754-2008 NaN encoding on MIPS
content:
## Summary

Add a new unstable compiler flag `-Zmips-nan2008` that enables the IEEE 754-2008 NaN encoding on MIPS targets by injecting the LLVM `+nan2008` target feature.

### Motivation

MIPS hardware and software ecosystems can be built with either the legacy MIPS NaN encoding or the IEEE 754-2008 NaN encoding. GCC's `-mnan=2008` flag selects the 2008 encoding, and some system ABIs (particularly for MIPS Release 6 cores and certain vendor toolchains) mandate it. When linking Rust code against C libraries or system code compiled with `-mnan=2008`, the NaN encoding must match across the entire binary to avoid runtime failures and undefined behavior.

Currently, Rust has no way to select the 2008 NaN encoding, making it impossible to interoperate with such ecosystems without resorting to custom target JSON specifications. This PR adds an explicit, architecture-gated unstable flag to enable the feature safely.

### What this PR does

- **New flag** `-Zmips-nan2008` (unstable): when set, injects `+nan2008` into the LLVM feature string for MIPS targets. The flag is only accepted on `mips`, `mips32r6`, `mips64`, and `mips64r6` architectures; attempting to use it on other architectures emits a fatal diagnostic (`MipsNan2008InvalidArch`).
- **Target modifier**: the option is registered with `[TRACKED] { TARGET_MODIFIER: MipsNan2008 }` in `options.rs`, so linking crates compiled with different values is a hard error by default (leveraging the existing target-modifier machinery). The error can be bypassed with `-Cunsafe-allow-abi-mismatch=mips-nan2008` if the user knows the ABIs are actually compatible.
- **LLVM feature injection**: in `llvm_util.rs`, the `llvm_features_by_flags()` function now checks `sess.opts.unstable_opts.mips_nan2008` and appends `+nan2008` to the feature vector when the target architecture is a MIPS variant; otherwise it emits the fatal diagnostic.
- **Docs**: unstable-book page at `compiler-flags/mips-nan2008.md` with usage examples and ABI compatibility warnings.

### Tests

- `tests/ui/target_modifiers/incompatible_mips_nan2008.rs` (+ auxiliary crate `mips_nan2008.rs`): verifies the target-modifier mismatch error is emitted when linking crates with conflicting `-Zmips-nan2008` settings, the error can be suppressed with `-Cunsafe-allow-abi-mismatch=mips-nan2008`, and matching settings compile cleanly. Mirrors the structure of `incompatible_fixedx18.rs`.
- `tests/codegen-llvm/mips-nan2008.rs`: checks that the `+nan2008` feature appears (or does not appear) in the LLVM `"target-features"` function attribute depending on whether the flag is set.
- Updated `compiler/rustc_interface/src/tests.rs` to track the new `mips_nan2008` option in the tracked-options test.

title: Add -Zllvm-target-feature to pass features directly to LLVM
content:
`-Ctarget-feature` passes unrecognized features through to LLVM with a warning.

Users who need LLVM-only features (e.g. the Linux kernel) must either tolerate the warning or resort to JSON target specs. 

This flag provides a dedicated mechanism, registered as a target modifier.

Tracking issue: rust-lang/rust#157753

title: Add a standalone reproducer attempt for rust-lang/rust#124105
content:
notify's CI on macOS intermittently dies with either the `closedir: Bad file descriptor` panic from rust-lang/rust#124105 or, when the caller has debug assertions enabled, a `fatal runtime error: IO Safety violation: owned file descriptor already closed` abort. Both come from the same event, a descriptor being closed by something that does not own it: `debug_assert_fd_is_open` runs immediately before the `closedir` whose assert rust-lang/rust#124105 is about, so which symptom appears depends only on whether `check_library_ub()` is active.

That issue has been open without anyone being able to reproduce it, so this is an attempt at a reproducer with no notify dependency, just the CoreServices FFI and std. Each round builds 4097 `dir_N/subdir` directories, creates an FSEventStream over all of them, schedules it on a run loop, calls FSEventStreamStart (which fails, a stream caps out around 4096 paths), invalidates and releases the stream, and then removes the tree with remove_dir_all while other threads hold ordinary File handles inside it.

Note that no stream is running during the removal. It is created, fails to start, and is released first. That is what the notify test actually does, so the suspect window is FSEvents' create/start-failure/release path rather than live event delivery.

Unverified: written on Linux, so it has only ever been type checked for x86_64-apple-darwin and never built or run. It is also a race, so a few hundred clean rounds would not say much either way.

Changes in this PR (apart from the LLVM update):
 * Updated cov-map tests due to minor ordering changes introduced in https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/commit/593103465326850f23bc9a6078ae7fb01065d46e. The affected tests are limited to LLVM >= 23 now.
 * Set `LLVM_VERSIONED_DYLIB_NAME_ON_DARWIN=OFF`, which restores the previous unversioned naming of the LLVM dylib on Darwin. I expect we'll want to change this for consistency with Linux, but given the amount of trouble Darwin dylibs have caused in the past, I'm not trying to do it in this PR.
 * Distribute the llvm-project/libc subproject, which is now a build dependency of LLVM.
 * Pull in f128 Windows ABI changes from https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/158778. These need to land in sync with the LLVM update (as ABI of libcalls is controlled by LLVM, not our ABI lowering).
 * Disable RISCV backend on dist-i686-mingw, because the build OOMs on a large generated file. This is a temporary measure until host tools are removed by https://github.com/rust-lang/compiler-team/issues/1020.
 * The llvm-project fork includes a new downstream patch for mingw: https://github.com/rust-lang/llvm-project/commit/b89cd8e6254701813a12a231d57b66228b998cf0 It works around mingw having broken TLS prior to GCC 16. (We're currently on GCC 14.)

title: Weird closure argument type inference error messages due to unexpected trait solver recursion
content:
Consider this code snippet. It admittedly looks a little silly, but that's because it has been minimized from [something much more complex](https://github.com/HadrienG2/hwlocality/issues/397).

```rust
use std::ops::Add;

struct Wrapper<T>(T);

impl<'a, T> Add<usize> for &'a Wrapper<T>
where
    &'a T: Add<usize, Output = usize>,
{
    type Output = usize;
    fn add(self, x: usize) -> usize {
        &self.0 + x
    }
}

fn main() {
    let _f = |x| &x + 42usize;
}
```

I would expect the build to fail with a clear type inference error, as there is no way to know what the type of the `x` argument of the `_f` closure is. Indeed both `x: usize` and `x: Wrapper<usize>` would work.

But instead, the build fails with an error that's only remotely related to the problem at hand as the trait solver reaches the recursion limit trying to determine if `Add` is implemented for infinitely nested `&Wrapper<Wrapper<Wrapper<Wrapper<...>>>`:

```text
$ cargo +nightly check
error[E0275]: overflow evaluating the requirement `&Wrapper<_>: Add<usize>`
  --> src/main.rs:16:21
   |
16 |     let _f = |x| &x + 42usize;
   |                     ^
   |
   = help: consider increasing the recursion limit by adding a `#![recursion_limit = "256"]` attribute to your crate (`reproducer`)
note: required for `&Wrapper<Wrapper<_>>` to implement `Add<usize>`
  --> src/main.rs:5:13
   |
 5 | impl<'a, T> Add<usize> for &'a Wrapper<T>
   |             ^^^^^^^^^^     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
 6 | where
 7 |     &'a T: Add<usize, Output = usize>,
   |                       -------------- unsatisfied trait bound introduced here
   = note: 126 redundant requirements hidden
   = note: required for `&Wrapper<Wrapper<Wrapper<Wrapper<Wrapper<Wrapper<Wrapper<Wrapper<_>>>>>>>>` to implement `Add<usize>`
   = note: the full name for the type has been written to '/home/hadrien/Bureau/reproducer/target/debug/deps/reproducer-d546312e19ea6546.long-type-4775855609470034830.txt'
   = note: consider using `--verbose` to print the full type name to the console

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0275`.
error: could not compile `reproducer` (bin "reproducer") due to 1 previous error
```

I am not 100% sure why this happens, but my guess is that the type inference engine somehow tries all possible types for `x` and this does not end well here as the list of types that this generic impl _might_ cover is infinite.

In any case, enabling the new trait solver leads to an error message that is much improved, as it now correctly explains that this is a closure argument type inference problem. But a secondary overflow error is still present, and it is even more mysterious now as there is no longer any hint of what is overflowing and why:

```rust
$ RUSTFLAGS='-Znext-solver' cargo +nightly check
    Checking reproducer v0.1.0 (/home/hadrien/Bureau/reproducer)
error[E0282]: type annotations needed
  --> src/main.rs:16:15
   |
16 |     let _f = |x| &x + 42usize;
   |               ^  -- type must be known at this point
   |
help: consider giving this closure parameter an explicit type
   |
16 |     let _f = |x: /* Type */| &x + 42usize;
   |                ++++++++++++

error[E0275]: overflow evaluating the requirement `&_: Add<usize>`
  --> src/main.rs:16:21
   |
16 |     let _f = |x| &x + 42usize;
   |                     ^

Some errors have detailed explanations: E0275, E0282.
For more information about an error, try `rustc --explain E0275`.
error: could not compile `reproducer` (bin "reproducer") due to 2 previous errors
```

So overall, I think some work on error message ergonomics is still needed here.


### Meta

`rustc --version --verbose`:
```
rustc 1.99.0-nightly (da86f4d07 2026-07-24)
```

(also present on 1.97 stable)

title: bootstrap: Split the `Step` trait into multiple traits
content:
- Revised version of https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/159423
- [#t-infra/bootstrap > Terminology consistency of the important concepts](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/326414-t-infra.2Fbootstrap/topic/Terminology.20consistency.20of.20the.20important.20concepts/with/611795947)
- [#t-infra/bootstrap > Path filters in bootstrap](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/326414-t-infra.2Fbootstrap/topic/Path.20filters.20in.20bootstrap/with/611415742)
---

An awkward thing about bootstrap's Step trait is that several of its implementations represent “helper tasks” that participate in bootstrap's internal caching system, but can't be explicitly selected via command-line arguments. Those tasks need to supply dummy implementations for some Step methods related to command-line processing.

This PR tries to reduce that tension by splitting the `Step` trait into two traits.

---

Steps that can be selected from the command-line implement the full `CommandLineStep` trait, which also provides an implementation of `Step`.

Helper tasks implement the smaller `Step` trait directly. They still participate in step-caching and step-tracing, but don't interact with command-line selectors.

Steps that can be selected from the command-line implement the full `CommandLineStep` trait, which also provides an implementation of `Step`.

Helper tasks implement the smaller `Step` trait directly. They still participate in step-caching and step-tracing, but don't interact with command-line selectors.

Type: Bug I created a workspace-level keybinding file at keybindings.json and added bindings for tasks such as: Ctrl+Alt+Shift+P → workbench.action.tasks.runTask with task label “Run Python Script” Ctrl+Alt+Shift+G → workbench.action.tasks.runTask with task label “Auto Stage + Commit + Push” The bindings are valid JSON and the workspace file is present. However, when the bindings are placed in keybindings.json, VS Code reports “No keybinding entries.” When the same entries are copied into the user-level C:\Users\\AppData\Roaming\Code\User\keybindings.json, they work. This indicates that workspace-level keybindings are not being loaded/applied in the current VS Code window even though the workspace folder and keybinding file are present. title: API: Ability dismiss own showInformationMessage/showErrorMessage
content:
<!-- ⚠️⚠️ Do Not Delete This! feature_request_template ⚠️⚠️ -->
<!-- Please read our Rules of Conduct: https://opensource.microsoft.com/codeofconduct/ -->
<!-- Please search existing issues to avoid creating duplicates. -->

<!-- Describe the feature you'd like. -->
Please add ability dismiss own messages.

Here is a use case:
Show error/information message when user entered none-existent path in the settings and remove the message when path is correct.
Yes, we can specify `type: "uri"` for the setting, but this will not allow user to leave the field blank or enter relative paths.

This will also allow us to create temporary messages that would hide themselves after some time.

Currently we can force to close all currently displaying messages by displaying same message 4 times in a short period of time, but that's just a hack that can't be used to dismiss one specific message.

title: Warn when NaN is passed as an aria-* attribute value
content:
## Summary

aria-* attributes currently bypass the NaN check in `ReactDOMUnknownPropertyHook` because they return early (line 97-99 of that file) before the check is reached. When a `NaN` number flows through, the DOM stringifies it to the literal string `"NaN"`, which is invalid for **every** ARIA attribute type and silently breaks accessibility.

This is a common pitfall when a computed numeric value is derived from user data or state that can be undefined/null:

```jsx
// e.g. items.findIndex(...) returns -1 → some derived math → NaN
<div aria-valuenow={computedValue} />  // renders aria-valuenow="NaN" — silent bug
```

**Changes:**

- `ReactDOMInvalidARIAHook.js` — extend `validateProperty` to accept the prop `value` and add a `NaN` check for valid, correctly-cased aria-* attributes. Mirrors the warning message already used by `ReactDOMUnknownPropertyHook` for non-aria attributes.
- `ReactDOMInvalidARIAHook-test.js` — three new test cases: NaN on a numeric aria attribute (`aria-valuenow`), NaN on a string-type aria attribute (`aria-label`), and no false-positive for valid integers.

## Test plan

- [x] `yarn test ReactDOMInvalidARIAHook` — all tests pass (new + existing)
- [x] Existing tests unaffected — only the `validateProperty` signature changes (internal)

title: Fix false hydration mismatch when client renders portal that returned null on server
content:
## Summary

Fixes #12615

When a component returns `null` on the server but renders a `ReactDOM.createPortal()` on the client, React was incorrectly emitting a hydration mismatch error:

```
Hydration failed because the server rendered HTML didn't match the client.
  <span>
    <HoverMenu>
+     <div>   ← false positive: this is portal content, not a span child
```

This is a false positive — the portal's `<div>` renders into a **separate container**, not into the parent `<span>`. It should not be compared against the parent's server HTML.

## Root Cause

When `updatePortalComponent` calls `pushHostContainer` to switch to the portal's container, the hydration state variables (`isHydrating`, `nextHydratableInstance`, `hydrationParentFiber`) were not reset. The portal's children then tried to claim hydration instances from the **parent container's** server nodes, which failed and triggered a mismatch error.

## Fix

Added two functions to `ReactFiberHydrationContext`:

- **`prepareToHydrateHostPortal`** — called in `updatePortalComponent` (begin work). Saves the current hydration state onto a stack and resets it, so portal children are inserted fresh rather than matched against server HTML.
- **`popHydrationStateAfterPortal`** — called in the `HostPortal` case of complete work. Restores the saved hydration state so the parent resumes hydrating correctly after the portal.

This correctly handles nested portals (via the stack) and cleans up on `resetHydrationState` (work loop interruption).

## Test Plan

- Added two new tests in `ReactDOMHydrationDiff-test.js`:
  - Portal renders to a separate container → no mismatch warning
  - Portal renders to the hydration root container → no mismatch warning
- All 39 hydration diff tests pass
- All 183 tests across `ReactServerRenderingHydration`, `ReactDOMServerPartialHydration`, and `ReactDOMFiber` suites pass

title: [compiler] Fix refs validation for forwarded ref props
content:
Fixes #35997

## Summary

This fixes a false positive in `react-hooks/refs` when forwarding a `ref` prop directly to JSX.

Previously, code like:

```tsx
function TextArea(props) {
  return <TextInput ref={props.ref} type="body" />;
}
```

was reported as:

`Cannot access refs during render`

even though the component was only forwarding the ref object to JSX and not reading `ref.current`.

The root cause was that `ValidateNoRefAccessInRender` validated all JSX attribute operands uniformly. That was too strict for the special `ref` prop, where passing a ref object through to JSX should be allowed.

This change teaches the validator to treat JSX `ref` attributes specially:

- still validate the JSX tag
- still validate non-`ref` JSX attributes
- still validate spread attributes and children
- skip direct-ref-value validation for the `ref` attribute itself

This preserves the existing error for actual render-time ref reads like `props.ref.current`, while allowing valid ref forwarding patterns.

## How did you test this change?

Reproduced the issue with a focused compiler fixture:

1. Add a fixture containing:

```js
// @validateRefAccessDuringRender @compilationMode:"infer"
function TextArea(props) {
  return <TextInput ref={props.ref} type="body" />;
}
```

2. Run:

```bash
corepack yarn workspace babel-plugin-react-compiler snap --pattern allow-forwarding-ref-prop-to-jsx --sync
```

Before the fix, this failed with:

```text
Error: Cannot access refs during render
...
return <TextInput ref={props.ref} type="body" />;
                         ^^^^^^^^^ Cannot access ref value during render
```

After the fix, the same targeted fixture passes:

```bash
corepack yarn workspace babel-plugin-react-compiler snap --pattern allow-forwarding-ref-prop-to-jsx --sync
```

I also checked the existing invalid fixture for reading `props.ref.current` to confirm the validator still rejects direct ref-value access during render.

title: [Flight] Performance track debug info is not recovered for plain object roots
content:
## Summary

`flushComponentPerformance` reads `root._debugInfo` from the chunk. When
that array is empty and the chunk is fulfilled, it recovers the debug info
from the resolved value, but only when the value is an array, an async
iterable, a React element, or a lazy:

```js
if (debugInfo.length === 0 && root.status === 'fulfilled') {
  const resolvedValue = resolveLazy(root.value);
  if (
    typeof resolvedValue === 'object' && resolvedValue !== null &&
    (isArray(resolvedValue) ||
      typeof resolvedValue[ASYNC_ITERATOR] === 'function' ||
      resolvedValue.$$typeof === REACT_ELEMENT_TYPE ||
      resolvedValue.$$typeof === REACT_LAZY_TYPE) &&
    isArray(resolvedValue._debugInfo)
  ) {
    debugInfo = resolvedValue._debugInfo;
  }
}
```

A plain object root is excluded, so the Server Components track in the
Performance panel does not work for payloads whose root is a plain object,
even when the resolved value carries a `_debugInfo` array. Verified in
`react-server-dom-webpack@19.3.0-canary-28cd4bb0-20260723`.

## Context

Waku's RSC payload root is a plain object mapping slot ids to elements
(`Record<string, unknown>`), which lets one payload carry several named
elements. This shape is deliberate and we would like to keep it. Today we
patch the read site with a build transform that drops the type restriction,
which works but is coupled to the compiled output:

https://github.com/wakujs/waku/blob/main/packages/waku/src/lib/vite-plugins/patch-rsdw.ts

@vitejs/plugin-rsc documents the same shape constraint for its performance
track example (vitejs/vite-plugin-react#1152, vitejs/vite-plugin-react#1304).

## Request

Relax the recovery to accept any object value that carries an own
`_debugInfo` array. The type restriction seems to mirror
`moveDebugInfoFromChunkToInnerValue`, where it guards attaching
`_debugInfo` to the value. The read site only reads the property, so the
restriction does not appear to protect anything there, and the relaxation
is additive: values without `_debugInfo` behave as before.

If there is a supported way to get the performance track with a plain
object root without reshaping the payload, that guidance would also
resolve this for us.

Bumps [axios](https://github.com/axios/axios) from 1.7.7 to 1.18.1.
Release notes

Sourced from axios's releases.

v1.18.1 — June 21, 2026

This release focuses on Node HTTP adapter fixes, safer AxiosError serialisation, runtime/type correctness fixes, documentation updates, and dependency maintenance.

🐛 Bug Fixes

  • AxiosError Serialisation: Made AxiosError#cause non-enumerable to prevent circular JSON serialisation failures when errors include nested causes. (#10913)
  • Node HTTP Adapter: Guarded socket.setKeepAlive for proxy agent streams, accepted path-only URLs when socketPath is configured, deferred environment proxy handling to Node, and explicitly passed maxBodyLength through to follow-redirects. (#10917, #10930, #10942, #10993)
  • Runtime and Type Correctness: Fixed several runtime crashes, type definition mismatches, and incorrect error handling paths. (#10959, #11021)
  • AxiosURLSearchParams: Switched the encoder callback to an arrow function so encoder.call(this) receives the AxiosURLSearchParams instance correctly. (#11019)

🔧 Maintenance & Chores

  • Documentation: Documented sensitive headers and status transition behaviour, prepared cleaned-up docs, added Deno install instructions, and clarified that request data is request-specific (#11007, #11010, #11023, #11025)

  • Dependencies: Bumped vite, rollup, form-data, js-yaml, and multer across the root project, docs, smoke tests, and module test workspaces. (#11011, #11012, #11013, #11014, #11015, #11016, #11017, #11026)

🌟 New Contributors

We are thrilled to welcome our new contributors. Thank you for helping improve axios:

  • @​webdevelopersrinu (#10913)
  • @​sijie-Z (#10993)
  • @​bartlomieju (#11023)
  • @​JSap0914 (#11019)

Full Changelog

v1.18.0 — June 13, 2026

This release hardens redirect and URL handling, improves the validateStatus configuration semantics, and includes updates to documentation, dependencies, and release metadata.

🔒 Security Fixes

  • Redirect Header Safety: Added Node HTTP adapter support for stripping caller-specified sensitive headers on cross-origin redirects, helping prevent custom auth headers such as API keys from leaking to another origin. (#10892)

  • URL And Request Hardening: Rejects malformed http: and https: URLs that omit // with ERR_INVALID_URL, while tightening prototype-pollution-safe config reads, stream size limits, FormData depth handling, data URL sizing, and local NO_PROXY matching. (#11000)

🐛 Bug Fixes

  • Status Validation: Added transitional.validateStatusUndefinedResolves so applications can opt in to treating validateStatus: undefined like the option was omitted, while validateStatus: null remains the explicit way to accept every status. (#10899)

🔧 Maintenance & Chores

  • Documentation: Published the v1.17.0 release notes, fixed a changelog typo, clarified the package update PR policy, and marked the proxy request config as Node.js-only in the advanced docs. (#10984, #10988, #10992, #10995)

  • Dependencies: Bumped @babel/core, @babel/preset-env, @commitlint/cli, @commitlint/config-conventional, @rollup/plugin-babel, @rollup/plugin-commonjs, @vitest/browser, @vitest/browser-playwright, eslint, lint-staged, rollup, vitest, and actions/checkout. (#10989, #10996, #10997)

  • Release Metadata: Prepared the 1.18.0 release by updating package metadata and the runtime VERSION value. (#11003)

title: [verified] fix(reconciler): recheck store snapshot after subscribe
content:
## Summary
- Problem: `useSyncExternalStore` can miss a post-subscribe snapshot repair when `Suspense` + `StrictMode` remounts a store consumer and the store mutates during `subscribe()` without notifying listeners.
- Why it matters: the hook contract expects a snapshot re-check after subscribing, but this remount path skipped that repair step.
- What changed: `subscribeToStore(...)` now re-checks the snapshot immediately after `subscribe(handleStoreChange)` returns and forces a rerender if the store changed during subscribe.
- What did NOT change (scope boundary): this does not change broader Suspense replay semantics or attempt to guarantee that no stale intermediate render is ever observed before the repair rerender.

## How did you test this change?
- `CI=1 npx -y yarn test useSyncExternalStore-test --runInBand`
- `CI=1 npx -y yarn test useSyncExternalStore --runInBand`

Related to: https://github.com/facebook/react/issues/35550

title: [DOM] Guard window.event reads in scheduler event tracking
content:
## Summary

Fixes #37100.

The DEV-only Performance Tracks instrumentation added in 19.2.0 reads `window.event` unconditionally in `trackSchedulerEvent()`, `resolveEventType()`, and `resolveEventTimeStamp()`. `trackSchedulerEvent()` runs at the entry of Scheduler-driven tasks (`performWorkOnRootViaSchedulerTask`, `processRootScheduleInImmediateTask`, and the passive-effects flush scheduled by `commitRoot`). These tasks live on deferred `setImmediate` ticks and can legitimately fire after a per-test-file DOM environment (jsdom / happy-dom under vitest or jest) has been torn down. When that happens the task throws `ReferenceError: window is not defined` before doing any work, which fails entire CI suites with an unhandled error attributed to the next, innocent test file.

This guards the three reads with `typeof window !== 'undefined'`, matching the bundle's existing convention for `window` accesses that may run outside a browser DOM (e.g. `canUseDOM`, the `window.ErrorEvent` detection in the error-reporting path). When `window` is gone the attribution resolves to `undefined`, i.e. "no event", which is accurate. `shouldAttemptEagerTransition()` and `resolveUpdatePriority()` are left untouched: they only run while an update is being dispatched, so `window` is alive by construction there.

## How did you test this change?

- Added a regression test (`ReactDOMWindowTeardown-test.js`, node environment + manually constructed JSDOM mirroring the issue's repro). It fails on `main` with `ReferenceError: window is not defined` from `performWorkOnRootViaSchedulerTask` and passes with this change.
- `yarn test ReactPerformanceTrack ReactDOMFiberAsync ReactDOMNativeEventHeuristic` — all pass.
- `yarn linc`, `yarn flow dom-node`, `yarn prettier` — clean.
- Ran the repro script from #37100 verbatim: against published `react-dom@19.2.8` it crashes as reported; against a locally built `NODE_DEV` bundle with this change it prints `done, no crash` and exits 0.

title: [Fiber] Don't reaquire HostSingletons during dev effect validation
content:
Stacked on #37112

In dev effects are validated using a double-invoke technique. To do this the effects are destroyed and recreated during a validation traversal. However this same disappear and reappear path is used when Offscreen Fibers go hidden and HostSingletons have unique behavior when going hidden. So now that the double invoke effects process happens during hydration it is more common to have your Singletons be released and acquired during this validation phase which is observable most notably by having extra attributes removed from them. The prior commits in this stack deal with preserving non-react owned attributes on release however it is semantically incorrect to release and acquire the singleton during this validation because it isn't really an effect, it simply lives in this traversal to avoid having to do another traversal during the commit.

This change adds a bit of info to the release and acquire path to only conditionally perform the necessary reacquire flow if we are not in the validation phase.

title: [Fiber] only remove properties from singletons on release
content:
Removing attributes does not actually reset all property state on the singleton instance. It also has the side effect of wiping any 3rd party set attributes and properties that 3rd party scripts and extensions.

Reimplements the singleton release to clear properties on the instance based on the last committed props for the singleton fiber.

Notably there is an unfixed path with preamble contribution markers that still just clears based on attributes which covers SSR'd attributes that need to be wiped before client recovery on hydration can continue. There are gated failing tests for this as a TODO.

title: net/http: HTTP/2 read loop spins at 100% CPU on a StreamError cached by tls.Conn
content:
### Go version

go version go1.26.5 linux/amd64

### Output of `go env` in your module/workspace:

```shell

GOSUMDB='sum.golang.org'
GOTELEMETRY='local'
GOTELEMETRYDIR='/home/runner/.config/go/telemetry'

GOTOOLCHAIN='local'
GOTOOLDIR='/opt/hostedtoolcache/go-6d471830/1.26.5/x64/pkg/tool/linux_amd64'
GOVCS=''
GOVERSION='go1.26.5'
GOWORK=''
PKG_CONFIG='pkg-config'
```

### What did you do?

An HTTP/2 `StreamError` can escape from one `net/http` transport through `Response.Body.Read`. If that body is used as the backing connection for another HTTP/2 transport, the outer transport mistakes the underlying error for a stream error parsed on the outer connection.

The following program uses only the standard library. It obtains a real net/http.http2StreamError from an inner HTTP/2 request, then returns it as a sticky read error from the connection backing an outer HTTP/2 request.

In the production case, the outer HTTP/2 connection runs over a `tls.Conn`, and that TLS connection runs over a `net.Conn` backed by another in-process HTTP/2 stream.

When the inner HTTP/2 stream is reset, its `http2StreamError` reaches `tls.Conn.Read`. `crypto/tls` treats this as a permanent input error and caches it. Every later call to `tls.Conn.Read` returns the same error without reading from the network.

The reproducer below uses `stickyConn` to model the observable behavior of a `tls.Conn` after it has cached the inner stream error. The
`http2StreamError` itself is obtained from a real standard-library HTTP/2 request rather than constructed by user code.

https://go.dev/play/p/IMjFU6ArpRU

(Should run this locally; running it on the playground will result in a deadlock error.)

Output:

```
inner error: http.http2StreamError: stream error: stream ID 1; INTERNAL_ERROR; received from peer
underlying Read calls in 100ms: 2253786
```

The process consumes approximately one CPU core until the connection is explicitly closed.

A real-world example is an in-process HTTP client running HTTP/2 over a `net.Conn` implemented using another HTTP/2 response body. No custom construction of the private error type is required.

### What did you see happen?

The outer HTTP/2 read loop continues reading after the underlying connection returns `http2StreamError`.

In the production path, the error propagation is:

```text
inner HTTP/2 RST_STREAM
    -> inner Response.Body.Read returns net/http.http2StreamError
    -> tls.Conn.Read receives the error
    -> crypto/tls caches the error without changing its concrete type
    -> every later tls.Conn.Read returns the same http2StreamError
    -> outer HTTP/2 read loop treats it as a locally parsed stream error
    -> the loop continues indefinitely
```

The relevant behavior in crypto/tls.(*Conn).readRecordOrCCS is effectively:

```golang
if c.in.err != nil {
	return c.in.err
}

// Read a TLS record from the underlying connection.
if err := c.readFromUntil(c.conn, recordHeaderLen); err != nil {
	if e, ok := err.(net.Error); !ok || !e.Temporary() {
		c.in.setErrorLocked(err)
	}
	return err
}
```

`http2StreamError` does not implement `net.Error`. Consequently, `halfConn.setErrorLocked` stores the original error directly rather than wrapping it in `tls.permanentError`:
```golang
func (hc *halfConn) setErrorLocked(err error) error {
	if e, ok := err.(net.Error); ok {
		hc.err = &permanentError{err: e}
	} else {
		hc.err = err
	}
	return hc.err
}
```

This detail is important: the cached error retains the concrete type net/http.http2StreamError, so the outer HTTP/2 read loop's direct type assertion succeeds on every iteration:
```golang
if se, ok := err.(http2StreamError); ok {
	if cs := rl.streamByID(se.StreamID, http2notHeaderOrDataFrame); cs != nil {
		rl.endStreamError(cs, se)
	}
	continue
}
```

After the first failure, no additional network traffic is required. The loop repeatedly calls `tls.Conn.Read`, receives the cached error, resets the read-idle timer when configured, checks the stream map, and continues. This consumes approximately one CPU core.

The caching behavior in `crypto/tls` is reasonable for a permanent transport error. The bug is that `net/http` cannot distinguish a `StreamError` parsed by the current Framer from an identically typed error returned by the Framer's underlying reader.

This assumes every `http2StreamError` was produced while parsing the current connection. An error originating from a lower HTTP/2 transport has the same concrete type, so it is treated as recoverable.

If the lower reader retains the error, as HTTP/2 response bodies and TLS connections may do, every subsequent read returns the same error and the loop spins indefinitely.

The server-side `terminalReadFrameError` check appears to have the same provenance issue.

### What did you expect to see?

A `StreamError` generated by the current Framer should remain recoverable and affect only its stream.

A `StreamError` returned by the `Framer`'s underlying `io.Reader` should be treated as a terminal connection read error. The read loop should exit and close the connection rather than reading again.

### Suggested fix

Distinguish errors originating from the underlying reader at the Framer I/O boundary. One minimal approach is to wrap only reader-provided `StreamError` values:

```golang
type frameReadError struct {
	err error
}

func (e frameReadError) Error() string { return e.err.Error() }
func (e frameReadError) Unwrap() error { return e.err }

type framerReader struct {
	io.Reader
}

func (r framerReader) Read(p []byte) (n int, err error) {
	n, err = r.Reader.Read(p)
	if _, ok := err.(StreamError); ok {
		err = frameReadError{err: err}
	}
	return n, err
}
```

The `Framer` constructor can wrap its reader once:
```golang
if r != nil {
	r = framerReader{Reader: r}
}
```

This covers frame headers, payloads, and recursive CONTINUATION reads. Locally parsed `StreamError` values remain direct values, while reader-originated errors become terminal to the existing direct type checks.

The wrapper preserves the error text and supports `errors.As` through `Unwrap`.

Regression tests should cover both cases:

The underlying reader returns `StreamError` while reading a frame header.
A valid frame header is read, then the underlying reader returns `StreamError` while reading the payload.
In both cases, the error should unwrap to `StreamError` but must be considered terminal by the HTTP/2 read loop.


`http2StreamError` does not implement `net.Error`. Consequently, `halfConn.setErrorLocked` stores the original error directly rather than wrapping it in `tls.permanentError`:
```golang
func (hc *halfConn) setErrorLocked(err error) error {
	if e, ok := err.(net.Error); ok {
		hc.err = &permanentError{err: e}
	} else {
		hc.err = err
	}
	return hc.err
}
```

This detail is important: the cached error retains the concrete type net/http.http2StreamError, so the outer HTTP/2 read loop's direct type assertion succeeds on every iteration:
```golang
if se, ok := err.(http2StreamError); ok {
	if cs := rl.streamByID(se.StreamID, http2notHeaderOrDataFrame); cs != nil {
		rl.endStreamError(cs, se)
	}
	continue
}
```

After the first failure, no additional network traffic is required. The loop repeatedly calls `tls.Conn.Read`, receives the cached error, resets the read-idle timer when configured, checks the stream map, and continues. This consumes approximately one CPU core.

The caching behavior in `crypto/tls` is reasonable for a permanent transport error. The bug is that `net/http` cannot distinguish a `StreamError` parsed by the current Framer from an identically typed error returned by the Framer's underlying reader.

This assumes every `http2StreamError` was produced while parsing the current connection. An error originating from a lower HTTP/2 transport has the same concrete type, so it is treated as recoverable.

If the lower reader retains the error, as HTTP/2 response bodies and TLS connections may do, every subsequent read returns the same error and the loop spins indefinitely.

The server-side `terminalReadFrameError` check appears to have the same provenance issue.

### What did you expect to see?

A `StreamError` generated by the current Framer should remain recoverable and affect only its stream.

A `StreamError` returned by the `Framer`'s underlying `io.Reader` should be treated as a terminal connection read error. The read loop should exit and close the connection rather than reading again.

### Suggested fix

Distinguish errors originating from the underlying reader at the Framer I/O boundary. One minimal approach is to wrap only reader-provided `StreamError` values:

```golang
type frameReadError struct {
	err error
}

func (e frameReadError) Error() string { return e.err.Error() }
func (e frameReadError) Unwrap() error { return e.err }

type framerReader struct {
	io.Reader
}

func (r framerReader) Read(p []byte) (n int, err error) {
	n, err = r.Reader.Read(p)
	if _, ok := err.(StreamError); ok {
		err = frameReadError{err: err}
	}
	return n, err
}
```

The `Framer` constructor can wrap its reader once:
```golang
if r != nil {
	r = framerReader{Reader: r}
}
```

This covers frame headers, payloads, and recursive CONTINUATION reads. Locally parsed `StreamError` values remain direct values, while reader-originated errors become terminal to the existing direct type checks.

The wrapper preserves the error text and supports `errors.As` through `Unwrap`.

Regression tests should cover both cases:

The underlying reader returns `StreamError` while reading a frame header.
A valid frame header is read, then the underlying reader returns `StreamError` while reading the payload.
In both cases, the error should unwrap to `StreamError` but must be considered terminal by the HTTP/2 read loop.

```go
package main

import "fmt"

type params struct{ k, l int }

var sink byte
var arr [56]uint32

//go:noinline
func fill(b []byte) {
	for i := range b {
		b[i] = byte(i)
	}
}

//go:noinline
func newThing(p params) []uint32 {
	// kl is computed in the entry block (kept there because it has uses in
	// two different blocks), lives in LO across the call to fill, and so
	// must be spilled from LO. The spill slot lands beyond the 32KB reach
	// of a MIPS 16-bit signed load/store offset because of scratch.
	kl := p.k * p.l
	var scratch [33000]byte
	if p.k > 0 {
		fill(scratch[:])
		sink = scratch[99]
		return arr[:kl]
	}
	return arr[kl:]
}

func main() {

	fmt.Println("ok:", len(s))
}
```

title: os: running SameFile on two character files or pipes will always return true on Windows
content:
### Go version

go version go1.26.4 windows/amd64

### Output of `go env` in your module/workspace:

```shell
set AR=ar
set CC=gcc
set CGO_CFLAGS=-O2 -g
```
